title: Women keep the world’s classrooms running. The teacher shortage asks them to carry even more.
subtitle: On the 60th anniversary of the international standard meant to protect teachers, governments again promised to elevate the profession. The test is whether that promise reaches the women who dominate early-years and primary teaching but remain underrepresented in leadership and are too often expected to absorb shortages through heavier work.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Sixty years after governments adopted an international standard on teachers’ pay, preparation, employment and working conditions, the organisations behind World Teachers’ Day asked them to “stand with teachers” again.

The appeal from UNESCO, the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International came as the profession confronted shortages, rising workloads and new demands created by technology, climate disruption, migration and displacement. The 1966 recommendation is now being revised. The anniversary was therefore not only a celebration; it was a test of whether standards written for another era can protect the people doing today’s classroom work.

For women, that question is especially consequential. They make up most of the world’s teachers at the levels where children first encounter formal education, yet their numerical presence has not translated into equal authority or consistently secure, well-paid work.
Fifty million teachers are needed by 2030

UNESCO’s 2026 data estimate that the world needs 50 million additional teachers by 2030 to provide universal pre-primary, primary and secondary education. Fifty-eight per cent of that demand is driven by teachers leaving the profession.

The figure is a projection, not a live count of empty classrooms. It is also broader than the 44-million estimate in UNESCO’s earlier Global Report on Teachers, which covered primary and secondary education. The two numbers should not be treated as contradictory measures of the same population: the newer total includes pre-primary education and uses updated data.

UNESCO reported annual attrition rates of 7.2% in pre-primary education, 4.7% in primary education and 5.4% in secondary education. Such global figures are assembled from national systems with different data quality and reporting schedules. They describe the scale of the challenge without identifying exactly where every vacancy exists.

Shortages can become self-reinforcing. When systems cannot recruit or retain enough qualified staff, the teachers who remain carry more work. Larger workloads can diminish wellbeing and make the profession less attractive to the next cohort.
A workforce built on women’s labour

The gender pattern is clearest in the earliest years. UNESCO reported that women made up 94% of pre-primary teachers, 68% of primary teachers, 58% of lower-secondary teachers and 52% of upper-secondary teachers in the data it published in 2023.

That concentration is not simply evidence of opportunity. Teaching young children has long been treated as an extension of women’s unpaid caring role. When socially essential work is coded as feminine, society can praise its moral value while resisting the salaries, staffing and professional autonomy required to sustain it.

UNESCO’s 2026 factsheet found that teachers were paid less than similarly qualified professionals across all education levels in 27 of the 68 countries analysed. That is not a global salary average, and it does not mean the pay gap is identical everywhere. It does show that the status problem is measurable, not merely symbolic.

Pay is only part of status. The 2026 observance distinguished teachers’ material standing—salary, workload and working environment—from their professional standing, including autonomy, support and a voice in policy. A system can increase recruitment targets while still losing teachers if it does not address all three.
Women fill classrooms but do not automatically reach the top jobs

The profession’s gender balance changes as authority increases. Older international survey data cited by UNESCO found women were 68% of lower-secondary teachers but 47% of school leaders. Country studies show that the gap can be wider, but the available figures cover different years and systems and should not be presented as one current global rate.

The evidence raises a question that many governments still cannot answer with recent, comparable information: when women form the majority of teachers, who becomes a principal, inspector, senior official or policy-maker?

The equality argument does not depend on claiming that women are naturally better leaders. It rests on whether promotion systems recognise experience fairly, whether rural postings and domestic responsibilities narrow women’s options, and whether harassment and violence make advancement unsafe.
Recruiting more teachers cannot mean normalising sacrifice

The solution is not to ask women to rescue education through vocation. Nor is it to treat the recruitment of men as a threat to women’s employment. A profession able to attract and retain people of different genders—and to move women into subjects and leadership roles where they are underrepresented—is more resilient than one built on the assumption that women will accept lower rewards because they care about children.

Governments can be judged against measures already embedded in the 1966 standard and renewed in current policy recommendations: competitive pay, secure employment, qualified preparation, continuing professional development, manageable workloads, safe workplaces, professional autonomy and participation in decisions.

They should also publish the evidence needed to see who benefits. That means teacher vacancies and turnover broken down by level, subject, location and gender; pay compared with similarly qualified work; the use of temporary or unqualified staff; promotion rates; and the share of leadership posts held by women. Recruitment announcements without retention data can conceal a revolving door.

For families, teacher policy is not an abstract labour dispute. It determines whether a child has a qualified adult in the room, whether that adult has time to notice who is falling behind and whether a school can keep experienced staff. For women working in education, it determines whether care is recognised as skilled public work—or treated as an endlessly expandable personal duty.

World Teachers’ Day’s anniversary message asked societies to elevate teachers’ status. The more exact demand is to stop relying on women’s commitment as a substitute for investment, authority and protection.
The Athena Perspective.
